sessions.title: Self-compassion break
script: If you've opened this pause, maybe something is weighing on you right now. You did well to stop for a moment.

Over the next few minutes, you'll move through three simple steps, inspired by the work of psychologist Kristin Neff. Three inner gestures you can come back to anywhere: at your desk, on the street, or lying awake in bed.
Settle in just as you are. Sitting, standing, it doesn't matter. If you like, close your eyes, or simply let your gaze rest on the floor in front of you.
Take a breath in through your nose, without forcing it.
[pause 3s]
And let the air flow out slowly, like a long sigh.
[pause 3s]
One more time. Breathing in… and letting go.
Now feel where your body is supported. Your weight on the chair or the floor. Your feet. Your hands, resting somewhere. Your body is being held up. You don't have to hold it.

Now choose something that's difficult for you at the moment. Something medium-sized, not the heaviest thing in your life. A worry at work, some tension with someone close to you, a concern that's been going round in your head since this morning.
Let the situation come to mind. Who's involved, what was said, what's worrying you.
Then, gently, turn your attention to your body. Where do you feel this difficulty? A tight throat, a weight on your chest, a knot in your stomach, a clenched jaw?
You don't need to change anything. You're simply noticing: ah, there it is.
You can even rest a hand on that spot, just to tell your body: I feel you. If it gets too intense, come back to your feet on the floor.
[pause 3s]
Step one: acknowledging. Say to yourself, in simple words: this is a moment of difficulty.
Or: this is hard right now. Or: this hurts. Choose the words that feel true for you.
This isn't complaining, and it isn't being dramatic. It's the opposite of pretending everything's fine. You're looking honestly at what's here, without adding to it.
Naming what hurts often helps you step back a little.
Step two: remembering that you're part of something bigger. Difficulty is part of life. It isn't proof that you're getting things wrong.
Say to yourself: other people go through this too. I'm not the only one who feels this way.

Right now, somewhere, someone is feeling overwhelmed in front of a full inbox. Someone is waiting for a reply that doesn't come. Someone is being hard on themselves, alone in a kitchen, late at night.
You don't know these people, and yet you share something with them. What you're feeling is deeply human.
This difficulty doesn't set you apart. If anything, it connects you to everyone who has ever found life heavy.
Step three: kindness. If it feels comfortable, place a hand on your heart. Or both hands. Or a hand on your cheek, on your belly, wherever that touch feels good.
Feel the warmth of your palm. The gentle pressure. Your chest rising and falling beneath it.
This gesture isn't trivial. Warm, gentle touch can help your body feel safe, a little like a friend's hand resting on your shoulder.
And now, say to yourself softly: may I be kind to myself. May I give myself the patience I need.
Repeat them slowly, once or twice, in time with your breath. Breathing in: may I be kind to myself. Breathing out: the patience I need.
These phrases are just an example. Ask yourself: what do I need, right here, right now? Comfort? Courage? Rest? A little understanding?
Imagine a friend going through exactly what you're going through. What would you say to them? Maybe: you're doing your best. Or: of course this is hard. Or simply: I'm here.
Take those same words, and offer them to yourself.
[pause 4s]

If nothing comes, that's fine. The intention is enough. And if an emotion rises, tears, a lump in your throat, that's normal too. You can slow down, open your eyes, or stop here. You're the one who decides.
Stay a moment longer with your hand where it is. Notice what's here now. Perhaps a little more space. Perhaps nothing has changed, and that's completely fine too.
Let your hand come down. Move your fingers a little, your shoulders. Come back to the sounds around you.
When the moment feels right for you, open your eyes.
These three steps fit into three short sentences. This is hard. I'm not alone in this. May I be kind to myself. You can carry them with you wherever you go.

sessions.title: After a mistake
script: Something went wrong. You forgot something, sent an email too fast, said something that hurt, missed an appointment. And ever since, it's been going round and round in your head.

Before anything else, notice this: if you're upset with yourself, it's because it matters to you. People, doing good work, the trust others place in you. This discomfort comes from something precious.
Over these six minutes, we won't erase what happened. Instead, you'll look at it clearly, without beating yourself up, and see what you can do with it.
Settle in. Place your feet flat on the floor. Let your hands rest on your thighs.
Breathe in gently through your nose.
[pause 3s]
And breathe out through your mouth, a little longer.
[pause 3s]
Once more, at your own pace. Let the out-breath carry away some of the tension in your shoulders.
And a third breath, just for you. There's nothing to fix during this one.
Feel your feet in contact with the floor. It's solid. Whatever happened, the ground is still there beneath you.
Now let the mistake come back to mind. Not replaying it on a loop, just placing it in front of you, like a photo on a table.
And notice what it does in your body. Shame and guilt often have a precise address. Heat rising in your face. A hollow feeling in your stomach. Shoulders curling forward, as if you wanted to hide.
You can simply name what you find: heat. Tightness. Heaviness. Without trying to push it away.
[pause 3s]
Now listen to what you've been telling yourself since the mistake. Maybe: I'm useless. I'm hopeless. I always ruin everything.
Look closely at the difference between two sentences. The first: I made a mistake. The second: I am a mistake.
The first is about an action. One specific moment, which can be understood and repaired. The second is about the whole of you, and it leaves no way out.
Guilt says: what I did wasn't right. It moves you to make amends. Shame says: I'm worthless. It makes you want to hide, or freeze.
If you hear that second sentence in your head, try rephrasing it. Bring it back to its true size. I forgot that file. I spoke too harshly. I made a mistake, on that day, in those circumstances.
Notice what changes in your body when the sentence shrinks back to its real size. Often, your chest breathes a little easier.
Now imagine a friend who knows you well and loves you unconditionally. They've heard the whole story. They sit down beside you.
They don't tell you it's nothing. They don't pretend. But they speak to you warmly.

Maybe they say: you were running on no sleep that day, you had a thousand things on your mind. Or: everyone gets things wrong, it doesn't take anything away from who you are. Or: I can see you're upset with yourself, and that shows how much this matters to you.
Listen to what they would say, in their own words. And let those words actually reach you.
Let them land the way a warm hand would on your shoulder. You don't have to agree with every word. Just let yourself hear them.
[pause 4s]
Notice if something loosens a little. Your shoulders, your belly, your breathing. Even a slight shift counts.
Notice, too, that you can hold two things at once: regret for what happened, and kindness toward the person who did it. One doesn't cancel out the other.
Now that you're a bit calmer, you can look at the situation with clearer eyes. What can be repaired?

Sometimes it's a sincere apology. Sometimes a message to correct some information, a phone call, an offer to catch up on what was delayed. Sometimes nothing can be repaired, and the only possible action is to do things differently next time.
Choose one single action. Small, concrete, doable. Picture yourself doing it: the time of day, the first words you'll say or write.
If it helps, decide when you'll do it. Today, tomorrow morning, right after lunch.
Writing it down can help, too.
[pause 3s]
Then gently ask yourself: what is this mistake teaching me? Maybe that you need to write important things down. To say no more often. To slow down before replying when you're running on empty.
One lesson, just one, is enough. You don't need to put yourself on trial.
Mistakes are how every human being learns. Including the people you admire most.
If you like, place a hand on your heart or your arm, and tell yourself: I made a mistake, and I still deserve kindness. Or, in your own words: I'm learning, like everyone else.
If strong emotions come up during this practice, that's normal. You can open your eyes, come back to your feet on the floor, or take a break. There's no rush.
Stay for a few more breaths with whatever you're feeling now. Without forcing yourself to feel better. Just being here, on your own side.
You've acknowledged the mistake. You know what you can repair. You've taken something from it. Whatever's left, you can leave behind.
Feel your back again, your hands, the sounds in the room. Have a little stretch if you feel like it.
And when the moment is right for you, open your eyes.
You're allowed to turn the page. Not because it didn't matter, but because you've done what needed doing.

sessions.title: Someone who matters
script: Hello. This practice is a little different from the others. There's no problem to solve here, no tension to undo. You're simply going to think about someone who matters to you.
When stress builds up, we tend to close in on ourselves. Remembering the connections that hold us up is a very simple way to feel supported, even when things are hard.
Settle in comfortably, with your back supported. Your eyes can close, or rest softly on a point in front of you.
Breathe in through your nose, letting your belly swell a little.
[pause 3s]
And breathe out slowly, as if you were blowing across a cup of hot tea.
[pause 3s]
Once more. Breathe in… and let it go.
Now let your breathing find its own rhythm. You don't need to guide it anymore. Just feel the air coming in, cool, and going out, a little warmer.
Notice where your body is resting, too. Your weight on the seat, your hands in your lap. There's nothing to get right here. Just a memory to let in.
Bring to mind someone who helped you at some point, in one way or another. Not necessarily the person closest to you. Maybe a grandmother, a childhood friend, a colleague, a teacher, a neighbor.
Don't look for the perfect person. Take the first one who comes, the one who brings a small smile inside.
If several faces appear, choose just one for today. The others can come back another time.
If no one comes right away, that's fine. You can think of someone who did you a simple kindness. A stranger who helped with a heavy suitcase, a pharmacist who took the time to listen.
[pause 3s]
Now try to see this person in detail. Their face. The color of their eyes. The shape of their smile, or that little crease between their eyebrows when they're thinking.
What are they wearing, in your memory? Where are they? Maybe in a kitchen, on a park bench, behind a desk, on the other end of the phone.
And their voice. The sound of it, the way they say your name. A phrase they often use.
Let this presence settle near you, as if they'd just sat down in the room. Notice what that changes already, simply imagining them here.
Now remember one particular moment when this person really mattered. One specific day.

Maybe they listened when things weren't okay. Maybe they believed in you before you believed in yourself. Maybe they did something quiet and kind: dropped off some soup, gave you a ride, sent a message at exactly the right time.
Bring that moment back as concretely as you can. Where were you? What time of day was it? What did they say, or do?
And what did you feel, in that moment? Relief, maybe. Surprise. The feeling of mattering to someone.

Ask yourself, too: what did this person pass on to me? A way of laughing at small troubles. Pride in doing things well. The idea that I was allowed to make mistakes. Perhaps even today, without realizing it, you carry a little of them in the way you are.
[pause 4s]
Now bring your attention to your chest. Is there something there? A warmth, a slight opening, a kind of fullness?
Gratitude is often felt in the upper body. Sometimes around the heart, sometimes in the throat, sometimes just as a smile at the corner of your mouth.
If you feel something, let it take up a little more room. Like a light being turned up slowly on a dimmer switch.
And if you don't feel anything in particular, that's completely fine. Thinking of them with care is already a lot. The feeling may come another time.

Sometimes an unexpected emotion rises, too. Nostalgia, or sadness, if this person is far away, or no longer here. That's normal. Meet it gently, and if it's too much, come back to your breath or open your eyes.
Now, silently, say thank you to them. A real thank you, in your own words.
You might say what you've never said out loud. Thank you for being there that day. Thank you for your patience. Thank you for believing in me.
If the words don't come, you can simply send them a look, a nod, the warmth you're feeling. They would understand.
Imagine they can hear you. See their face as they receive your words. Maybe they smile, or look surprised, a little moved.
If you like, rest a hand on your chest as you thank them. As if to keep this moment close.
[pause 4s]
Stay with this warmth for a few more breaths. Notice how simply thinking about someone can change the atmosphere inside you.
You're part of a web of connections. People have supported you. And you too, without always knowing it, have mattered to others.
Research suggests that regularly bringing this kind of gratitude to mind can help us feel more connected to others. And connection is one of our best buffers against stress.
Gently, let the image fade. Come back to your breath, to your body resting here, to the sounds around you.
Move your hands and feet a little. And when the moment feels right, open your eyes.
One last idea to take with you. What if you told them today? A message of just a few words is enough. You might be surprised by the difference it makes, on both sides.

sessions.title: For those who care for others
script: You spend a large part of your days looking after other people. A child who wakes up in the night, an aging parent, a partner who's unwell, patients, pupils. These few minutes are for you.

Caring for others wears you down. Not because you're not good enough. Simply because giving, day after day, takes an enormous amount of energy. Feeling that strain isn't a weakness. It's a sign of how much you give.
If you've managed to find a few minutes on your own, wonderful. And if you're listening to this in a waiting room, or with a child playing next to you, that's fine too. Work with what's possible.
Make yourself as comfortable as you can. Let your back lean into something. For once, you're the one being held.
Take a breath that's a little fuller than usual.
[pause 3s]
And let it out slowly, without holding anything back.
[pause 3s]
Once more. And as you breathe out, let your shoulders drop a little.
Let the out-breath be a little longer than the in-breath, like a quiet sigh of relief.
Bring your attention to your hands. These hands that carry, wash, cook, reassure. For now, they have nothing to do. Let them rest, open or lying on your thighs.
Your breath takes care of you too, without you having to think about it. In and out, day and night. Let it do its work for a few moments.
Now notice the tiredness that's here. Maybe a heaviness in your legs, stinging eyelids, tension between your shoulder blades, or a fog in your head.
You might even place a hand where the tiredness is strongest, the way you would for someone else.
You don't have to fight it, or hide it. Here, nobody needs you to be on top form. You can simply tell yourself: yes, I'm exhausted, and that makes sense after everything I carry.

If other emotions come along with the tiredness, irritation, sadness, sometimes even resentment toward the person you care for, let them be here too. They aren't bad feelings. They're human feelings, telling you that your resources have limits.
Let these feelings simply be here for a few breaths, without sorting them. You can tell yourself: this is heavy right now. And that's understandable.
Now let's try a very simple practice, using the breath. It rests on one idea: your compassion needs to flow in both directions. Toward the other person, and toward you.

To begin, focus only on the in-breath. With each breath in, imagine you're taking in some kindness for yourself. A warmth, a soft light, or just the word "rest". Whatever you need, right here, right now.
Breathe in for you.
[pause 3s]
And again. Feel that kindness spreading through your chest, your belly, all the way into your tired arms.
[pause 3s]
You're allowed to receive. Even if you're not used to it. Even if a small voice tells you others need it more than you do.
Now bring to mind the person you care for. Or several people, if that's your situation. See their face, as it is today.
And add the out-breath. As you breathe in, you take in kindness for yourself. As you breathe out, you send kindness toward them.
One for me, one for you.
You don't need to picture anything specific. The intention is enough. You can imagine the air that surrounds you both. The same room, the same air, shared.
If thinking of this person stirs up worry, come back first to your in-breath, for you. Your own steadiness comes first.
Breathe in for you. Breathe out for them.
[pause 4s]

You can adjust the balance depending on what you feel. If your reserves are especially low, keep several breaths for yourself before sending one toward them. If it's worry for them that's strongest right now, direct more of your breath their way.
There's no right ratio. Let your breathing find its own balance, like a tide coming in and going out.

You can carry on like this for a few breaths. Breathing in, kindness for me. Breathing out, kindness for you. If your mind drifts to your to-do list, that's normal. Bring it back, without blame, to the next breath.
Now here's a phrase that may help ease the guilt of never doing enough. Listen to it, and repeat it silently if it speaks to you.
I'm doing my best. I can't control everything.
Their suffering isn't entirely in my hands. My love, yes. My presence, yes. But not everything else.
This is sometimes called finding the right distance. Staying close and attentive, without carrying on your shoulders what isn't yours to carry.
You can care deeply, and still put some things down.
Let these words settle. Notice what they do in your body. Maybe relief, maybe some resistance. Both are normal.
If you prefer, find your own words. I'm already doing a lot. I'm here, and that already counts for so much. I'm not responsible for everything.
If a strong emotion rises, tears perhaps, let it pass through. You can also open your eyes and take a break. There's nothing to get right.
[pause 3s]
Before we finish, think of one small thing you could do for yourself today. Really small, realistic, given the day you have ahead.
Drinking a hot coffee without rushing, for once. Ten minutes' walk outside. Calling a friend. Asking someone to take over one task. Going to bed a little earlier.
Choose one. And picture it, already done. It isn't a luxury. It's what allows you to keep on giving.
If you like, place a hand on your heart as you choose. Like a small promise to yourself, with no pressure. And if the day has other plans, you can try again tomorrow.
Stay a moment longer with your breath, without guiding it at all. Notice how you feel now, without expecting a miracle.
Gently bring your attention back to the room. The sounds, the light, the contact of your body with the seat.
Move your neck a little, your shoulders. And when the moment is right, open your eyes.
Remember today: taking care of yourself is part of your role. You can't pour from an empty cup.
And tonight, if you think of it, just take a few breaths like this one more time: one for me, one for you.

sessions.title: Make peace with your body
script: You and your body may not always get along. There's the mirror, the photos, the clothes that feel tight. Sometimes there's illness, pain, a tiredness that won't lift. Or simply the feeling that it doesn't do what you'd like it to.

This practice doesn't ask you to love your body overnight. That would be asking too much. It invites you to try, for a few minutes, a different way of looking at it: less like a judge, more like someone saying thank you.

Find a position that's truly comfortable. Lying on your back, curled up in an armchair, wrapped in a blanket if you like. Adjust anything that bothers you: a cushion under your knees, a looser waistband.
Close your eyes if that feels pleasant. Otherwise, let your gaze rest on a neutral spot.
Breathe in gently through your nose.
[pause 3s]
And breathe out, letting the weight of your body sink into whatever is holding you.
[pause 3s]
One more breath, a little slower.
Let it reach down into your belly, then leave without any hurry.
Then let your breathing happen on its own. Simply feel the movement it creates: your belly or chest rising, then falling.
Feel too the places where your body meets what supports it. Your heels, your back, the back of your head. There's nothing you need to hold up.
Before we begin, you might notice something. As soon as the body comes up, thoughts often arrive all by themselves. Too much of this. Not enough of that. I should. If only.

You don't have to silence them. You don't have to believe them either. You can just recognize them, like people passing in the street: oh, there's the judgment about my stomach. Oh, there's the comparison.
Then, without arguing with them, come back to sensation. Not to the image of your body, but to what it feels, from the inside.
Each time a judgment pulls you back to the mirror, that's okay. Just return to what you can feel: warmth, weight, contact.
[pause 3s]
Start with your feet. Feel their contact with the floor, the bed, or the fabric of your socks. Maybe warmth, coolness, a slight tingling.
Wriggle your toes a little, if you like, just to feel them more clearly.

These feet have carried you for years. They took your first steps. They took you to school, to work, to appointments that mattered. They've walked on sand, on wet pavements, perhaps down hospital corridors.
They did all that without asking for thanks. So, silently, simply tell them: thank you for carrying me.
[pause 3s]
Move gently up to your legs, your knees, your hips. All this architecture that lets you get up in the morning, climb the stairs, run for a bus.
If part of your legs hurts, or doesn't work the way it used to, you can still greet it. Thank you for everything you've done, and for what you still do.
You can rest a hand on your thigh as you say it, as a small gesture of respect.
Now move to your hands. Feel them, resting. The palms, the fingertips, the small sensations living there.
Think of everything they do each day. They type on a keyboard, open doors, chop vegetables, hold a phone, write your name. They stroke a cat, hold a child's hand, comfort someone who's crying.
And your arms. They've carried shopping bags, moving boxes, maybe a sleeping baby. They've let you hold people close.
Thank you, hands. Thank you, arms. For everything you do that I so rarely notice.
If your hands are stiff or sore today, you can thank them anyway, and let them rest completely.
Maybe you notice a little warmth in your palms, or simply their weight. This is how gratitude for the body begins: by actually feeling it, rather than looking at it from the outside.

Now bring your attention to the center of your chest. Somewhere underneath, your heart is beating. You may not feel it directly, and that's okay. You can rest a hand there if you like, to feel a little closer.

This heart has been beating since before you were born. Around a hundred thousand times a day. It has never stopped to rest. It beat through your calmest nights and your hardest days. It's beating right now, for you, asking nothing in return.
And your breath. These lungs filling and emptying, thousands of times a day. Even when you're angry with your body, it keeps on breathing for you.
Take a moment to recognize this loyalty. Thank you, heart. Thank you, breath.
You can let these words ride on your breath. Thank you on the in-breath. Thank you on the out-breath.
[pause 4s]
Now, if you feel able, choose an area of your body you have a more difficult relationship with. Somewhere you judge, or hide, or that hurts.
If that feels too charged today, you can stay with your heart or your hands. You have nothing to prove.
If you do choose an area, simply rest your attention on it, delicately. The way you'd approach a slightly timid animal. Not too fast.
Notice the emotions that come. Embarrassment, sadness, sometimes anger. They often have a long history. Let them be here, without judging yourself for feeling them.
Then, if you can, send this area a little kindness. You can rest a hand on it. Or imagine a warmth wrapping around it, like a soft, warm blanket.
Breathe gently toward it. As if each breath in brought a little more room, and each breath out let a little tension go.
And tell it, in your own way: I'm sorry I've been so hard on you. Or: you're part of me. Or simply: I'm here.
You don't need to believe it completely. It's an intention, a seed. It will grow in its own time.
[pause 4s]

If strong emotions have come up, that's completely normal. The body holds a lot. You can stop at any moment, open your eyes, come back to your breathing. And if your relationship with your body has been painful for a long time, talking to a professional can really help.
Now take a moment to feel your body as a whole. From your feet to your head. Not a perfect body. A living body, breathing, feeling, keeping you company.
This body has changed, and it will keep changing. It has been through years, scars, transformations. And it has never stopped being yours.
Notice whether there's a little more gentleness than at the start. Or perhaps not. Both are okay.
You won't keep this softer way of seeing all the time. Old judgments will come back. But each time you thank a part of yourself, even briefly, you're training a different habit.
[pause 3s]
Gently begin to move. Your toes. Your fingers. Maybe a small stretch, like a cat waking up, just whatever feels good.
Listen to the sounds around you. Sense the light through your eyelids.
Take a slow breath, and feel your whole body breathing with you.
And when the moment is right for you, open your eyes.
Today, the next time you catch yourself judging your body, try this little phrase: thank you for carrying me. This body isn't your enemy. It has been your ally from day one.

sessions.title: Soften your inner critic
script: Inside each of us there's a little voice that comments on everything. It reads your emails over your shoulder, it counts your mistakes, it compares. Sometimes it whispers, sometimes it shouts.
Today, we're not going to try to silence it. We're going to get to know it, understand what it's after, and answer it with another voice, a gentler one, that's also yours.
Find a position where your body feels both steady and relaxed. Your back upright without stiffness, your shoulders dropping, your hands resting.
Close your eyes if you like, or simply lower your gaze.
Breathe in through your nose, calmly.
[pause 3s]
Breathe out through your mouth, as if you were fogging up a window.
[pause 3s]
Once more. Let the air leave a little more slowly than last time.
Now let your breathing return to normal. Choose a place where you can feel it clearly: your nostrils, your chest, your belly. Stay there for a few moments, with this simple coming and going.
If your mind wanders off, that's normal. Just bring it back, without comment. That's already a small training in kindness.
Each return to the breath is a bit like a hand on your shoulder. You don't scold yourself for wandering. You just come back.
Now let a typical sentence from your inner critic come to mind. A sentence you know by heart, because you hear it so often.

Choose one that stings a little, but not the most painful one. For example: you'll never manage it. Late again, it's always the same with you. Everyone's going to see you don't know what you're doing. You should have done better.
Hear it in your head, in its exact words. Don't correct it straight away. Listen to it, the way you'd listen to someone talking in the next room.
[pause 3s]
Now notice the tone of this voice. Is it curt? Contemptuous? Impatient? Does it sound like someone you've known, a parent, a teacher, a former boss?
You don't need to analyze it. Just notice whether it feels familiar.
And notice its effect on your body. Maybe your chest tightens. Your head sinks into your shoulders. Your stomach knots, or you suddenly feel like disappearing.

Interesting, isn't it? A few words in your head, and your whole body reacts as if facing a threat. That's exactly what's happening: your system goes on alert, as if you were under attack. Except the attack is coming from the inside.
Take a moment to rest a hand on the place that's reacting most. Just to tell your body: I can see this hurts.
Let your breathing slow a little under your hand. You're not fighting the voice. You're looking after the one who hears it.
[pause 3s]
Now, a slightly surprising question. What is this voice trying to protect?
Because the inner critic, however harsh, often has an intention. A clumsy one, but a real one. It wants to spare you rejection. Embarrassment in front of others. Losing your place. Failing.
Maybe it learned, a long time ago, that to be accepted, you had to be flawless. And it's still trying to keep you safe, with the only tools it knows: fear and pressure.
Research on self-criticism suggests this kind of pressure tends to drain motivation rather than build it. Encouragement usually works better than threats, for adults as much as for children.
Ask it silently: what are you afraid of, for me? And let the answer come, without searching for it. A word, an image, a sensation.
[pause 4s]
If something came up, you can acknowledge it. Ah, so that's it. You're afraid I won't measure up. You're afraid people will let me down.
And if nothing came, that's fine. Simply asking the question already changes your relationship with this voice a little.
Sometimes the answer arrives later, while you're doing the dishes or walking somewhere.
Now imagine a very dear friend comes to see you. Someone you love deeply. With a lump in their throat, they say: I'll never manage it. I'm always late, it's always the same with me.
Would you answer: yes, that's true, you're hopeless? Of course not.
So what would you say? In what tone? Maybe you'd put a hand on their arm. Maybe you'd say: hey, you're exhausted right now. You're doing so much. Being late once doesn't define who you are.
Listen to your own voice when it speaks to someone you love. Its warmth, its patience, its quiet firmness too.
Notice that kindness isn't the same as letting yourself off the hook. A good friend can still encourage you to do better. They just don't crush you to get there.
Take a moment to feel that voice inside you. Picture your friend's face as they listen, and soften a little. Notice whether your own breathing changes when you speak this way.
Now we're going to rephrase your critic's sentence. Not to deny it, or to pretend everything's fine. But to keep the useful idea, and change how it's said.
Take the original sentence. Ask yourself: what does it really want for me? Often, behind "late again", there's: I'd like you to be reliable, so people can count on you.
So the kind voice might say: you care about being reliable, and that's a lovely quality. What would help you leave earlier tomorrow?

Behind "you'll never manage it", there may be: I'm afraid you'll be disappointed. And the gentle voice would say: this is hard, and you're allowed to take it step by step. You've already got through difficult things before.
Now it's your turn. Take your own sentence, and rephrase it the way you would for that friend. Keep what's true in it. Change the tone.
[pause 5s]
Take your time. If the words don't come, start simply with: I can see this is hard for you. The rest can follow.
Say this new sentence to yourself again, slowly, silently. Perhaps with your hand on your heart. Notice how your body receives it.

Maybe a little relaxation. Maybe some resistance, a part of you saying: that's too nice, I don't deserve it. That's very common, especially at first. It isn't a failure. It's like learning a new language: the first words sound strange, then they become familiar.
And if this practice stirs up strong emotions, that's normal. You can open your eyes, breathe, stop here. You can come back whenever you like.
[pause 3s]
Stay a few more breaths in this space. The critical voice may still be there, somewhere. But you've heard something else.
You don't have to choose between the two once and for all. You're simply discovering that you get to choose the tone.
Because this gentle voice isn't borrowed. You already use it every time you comfort someone. It belongs to you too. You're simply allowed to turn it toward yourself.
Bring your attention back to your breathing, then to your whole body. Gently move your fingers, your toes. Stretch your neck.
When the moment is right for you, open your eyes and look around.
Today, when the critic speaks up, just try asking yourself: would I talk like this to someone I love? And if the answer is no, try the other voice.

sessions.title: Lonely tonight
script: Tonight, loneliness is making itself felt. Maybe the flat is too quiet. Maybe your phone hasn't buzzed all evening. Or maybe there are people all around you, and you still feel on the outside.
You did well to come here. For these few minutes, we're going to keep this feeling company, instead of running from it.

First, something important: loneliness hurts, and that's no accident. The need for connection is as basic as the need to eat or sleep. When it isn't met, the body registers it as an alarm. What you're going through isn't a flaw. It's a human signal, and a completely legitimate one.
Settle in wherever you are. On the sofa, in bed, against a cushion. If you have a blanket or a hot drink nearby, bring them closer. Your comfort matters.
Let your eyes close, or keep a soft light somewhere in view.
Breathe in slowly.
[pause 3s]
And let the air out, without hurrying.
[pause 3s]
Once more, feeling your chest rise, then fall.
And a third one, very gentle, letting your shoulders grow a little heavier.

Notice where your body is in contact with things. The weight of your legs. Your back leaning against something. The texture of the fabric under your fingers. Tonight, something is holding you up, quite literally.
Listen to the sounds as well. A car in the distance, the hum of the fridge, maybe rain. The world is still there, all around you.
Let those small sounds keep you company for a moment. You don't have to do anything with them.
[pause 3s]
Now, if you're willing, look for where loneliness lives in your body. It often has a shape. An emptiness in the chest. A tight throat. A coldness, or a heaviness in the arms.
There's no right or wrong way for loneliness to feel. Whatever you find is welcome.
Don't try to make it go away. Just rest your attention on it, gently. As if you were sitting down next to someone who's sad, without saying a word.
You can place a hand there. Feel the warmth of your palm. You're the one offering this touch, and it counts.
Breathe toward that place. Imagine that with each breath in, a little space opens up around the feeling. Like opening a window in a room that's been closed for too long.
You can tell yourself softly: I feel lonely tonight, and it's hard. Use whatever words feel like yours.
Saying it plainly often softens it a little. You're no longer pretending, and no longer fighting it.
[pause 3s]
Now widen your view a little. Imagine your street, your neighborhood, your city, seen from above, at night. Thousands of lit windows.
Some dark, some glowing blue from a screen, some warm and yellow.

Behind many of those windows, someone is feeling just what you're feeling right now. A student far from home, eating a bowl of pasta in front of a laptop. An elderly man watching television without really seeing it. A young mother rocking her baby at two in the morning, feeling invisible. Someone who's just moved to a city where they don't know a soul.
None of these people know each other. And yet tonight, they share something with you. Loneliness, strangely enough, is one of the most widely shared experiences in the world.
And it says nothing about your worth. It only says that a need is waiting to be met. Even people surrounded by others feel lonely on certain evenings.
You're not the only one feeling this. Let that idea settle.
[pause 4s]
Let's send them something. Not a message, not a call. A simple wish, from your heart.
Think of all those lit windows, and silently tell them: may you feel less alone tonight. May someone be thinking of you. May you find a little warmth.

And now turn that same wish toward yourself, since you're one of those windows too. May the loneliness weigh a little less tonight. May I find warmth, inside me and around me. May I know that I matter.
If these words sound strange, that's normal. Just hold on to the intention, like a candle being lit.
You might picture that small flame passing from window to window, right across the city.
This flame doesn't rest on you alone. Every window that receives it keeps it going in turn. And perhaps, somewhere, someone is thinking of you in the very same way.
[pause 3s]

Now let a memory of connection come back. A moment when you felt a real bond with someone. It doesn't have to be a big moment. A fit of giggles with a colleague. A noisy family dinner. A long conversation on a train platform. A knowing look shared with a stranger.
Relive that moment in detail. Where were you? What were the sounds, the smells, the light? Who was there, and what was being said?
And above all, find what you were feeling. That warmth, that lightness, that sense of belonging.
Notice where that warmth sits in your body. Maybe in the very same place as the emptiness from earlier. Let it settle there for a moment.
Your body remembers this feeling. It's capable of feeling it. And it will feel it again.
Let yourself rest in it for a few breaths, the way you'd lean against someone you trust.
If this memory also brings some sadness, because that person is far away, or that time has passed, let it be here. Sadness and warmth can live side by side.
[pause 3s]
Before we finish, think of one tiny act of connection you could do tomorrow. Nothing spectacular.

Send a message to someone you've been thinking about. Really say hello to the person at the bakery, looking them in the eye. Invite a colleague for a coffee. Call a grandparent. Sign up for that activity you've been tempted by for ages.
Choose one. Picture yourself tomorrow, doing it. It isn't much, and that's often how connections start again.
If that feels like too much tonight, simply keep the idea in mind. That's already a beginning.
Studies on social connection suggest that it's often these small, everyday interactions, repeated over time, that build a sense of belonging.
For now, gently come back to your breath, the air flowing in and out. You're here, with yourself, and that is a real presence.
Stay a moment longer with your hand resting on you, and your breath coming and going. Notice how you feel now. Without needing the loneliness to be gone.
If it's still here, that's okay. Tonight, you didn't leave it on its own. You kept it company.
You can tell yourself, if it feels right: I'm staying with myself tonight.
And if this feeling of loneliness comes back often, or weighs very heavily, talking to a health professional can be a real source of support.
Gently, come back to the sounds of the room, the contact of your body. Move your hands a little.
And whenever you like, open your eyes, or let yourself drift toward sleep if it's time.
Tonight, thousands of people believe, just like you, that they're alone. You're not set apart from anyone. And somewhere, someone will be glad to hear from you tomorrow.

sessions.title: Letting go of a grudge
script: A grudge is a bit like a stone in your shoe. At first, you feel it with every step. Then you get used to it, you limp a little without noticing. And you forget that you could take it out.
Over the next ten minutes, you'll look at a grudge you've been carrying, and see whether you can lighten the load a little. For you. Not for the other person.

One important note before we begin. Choose a light or moderate grudge. A hurtful remark from a colleague, a friend who didn't keep their promise, a family member who broke your trust. Not a situation involving violence, and not a trauma. Wounds like those deserve to be explored gently, with the support of a professional.
And nothing obliges you to forgive. Not today, not ever. Here, you go at your own pace, and you can stop at any time.
Settle into a steady position. Feet on the floor, back supported, hands resting on your thighs or your belly.
If you like, close your eyes. Otherwise, keep a soft gaze, resting downward.
Breathe in through your nose, deeply but without forcing.
[pause 3s]
And breathe out slowly, through your mouth.
[pause 3s]
Once more. Breathe in… and breathe out, letting your jaw loosen.
Now let your breath find its own rhythm. Rest your attention on your belly, rising slightly as you breathe in, and softening as you breathe out.
Feel the weight of your body. Your hips on the seat. Your feet on the floor. You're here, safe, in the present moment. What happened belongs to the past. All you're going to do now is look at it.
If at any point what comes up feels too strong, come back to this anchor: your feet, your belly breathing. It will always be there.
You can try it right now: press your feet gently into the floor, then let go. That's your safe place for the whole session.
[pause 3s]
Now let the situation come to mind. The person, the moment, the words or actions that hurt you.
You don't need to relive it all in detail. One image is enough. A fragment of the scene, like a blurry photo.

And notice what happens in your body as you think about it. A grudge often has a physical signature. A clenched jaw. Heat in the chest. Fists that want to close. A knot in the stomach, pulling tighter.
You can name what you feel. Anger. Sadness. Disappointment. Humiliation, perhaps. Every emotion has the right to be here.
Let these emotions exist without feeding them. You don't need to replay the scene to feel them. If it gets intense, take one breath down into your belly, then look again.
[pause 3s]
Now acknowledge the hurt. Not to dwell on it, but to do it justice.
Say to yourself silently: what happened hurt me. I had every right to be hurt. My reaction makes sense.
Often, we hold on to a grudge because it feels as if no one has ever acknowledged what we went through. So start there. You acknowledge it.
Perhaps what hurt was a need that wasn't respected. The need for respect, for being listened to, for being taken into account. That need was legitimate. It still is.
Place a hand on your heart if it helps, and let that acknowledgment reach you.
[pause 3s]
Now look honestly at what this grudge is costing you. You.

How many times have you gone back over that scene? In the shower, on the train, as you're falling asleep? How many imaginary conversations have you had with this person, searching for the perfect comeback?
And in your body, every time you think about it, the tension comes back. Your heart speeds up, your muscles tighten. As if the event were happening again, over and over.

Notice, too, whether this grudge spills over into other parts of your life. A greater wariness of other people. An irritability that flares up without warning. A subject you avoid, a place you no longer go.
Meanwhile, the other person probably feels none of this. You're the one carrying the weight. Like holding a bag of stones at arm's length, hoping it will feel heavy to someone else.
Just notice that. Without blaming yourself. Holding a grudge is a very human way of protecting yourself. It may have served you, for a while.
You can thank that protection, silently. Thank you for looking out for me. And gently ask yourself: do I still need to hold it this tightly?
[pause 3s]
So what is forgiveness, really? Not what we often think.
Forgiving isn't excusing. What happened wasn't acceptable, and it still isn't.
Forgiving isn't forgetting. You can keep the memory, and the lesson that comes with it.
Forgiving doesn't necessarily mean reconciling. You can forgive someone and decide not to see them again. You can forgive and keep your boundaries, firmly.
Forgiving doesn't mean forcing yourself to feel affection, either. You can stay neutral toward this person. You can even go on not liking them.
Forgiving means putting the weight down. Deciding that this story won't take up so much room inside you anymore. Taking back the energy it's been using up.
It's a gift you give yourself, far more than one you give them.
Sometimes it helps to remember that the other person was also acting with their own limits, their fears, their tiredness. That doesn't excuse them. It simply makes them human, like you.
Take a breath with that idea. Not to change your mind about what happened. Just to see whether the fist inside you can loosen, even a notch.
[pause 3s]
Now see whether you can take one tiny step in that direction. Not a grand gesture. Just an opening.

You can choose a phrase, if one of them speaks to you. For example: I choose to put this weight down, a little. Or: I don't condone what you did, but I no longer want to carry it. Or: I'm freeing myself from this story, at my own pace.
If no phrase feels right, simply keep the intention. The wish, however timid, to feel freer one day.
And if you sense it isn't the right time, that the anger still needs to exist, that's completely fine too. You can say: not yet. And that in itself is a form of honesty with yourself.
Imagine setting the bag of stones down on the ground, beside you. It's still there, you can pick it up again if you want. But for now, your arms can rest.
Feel your arms, your shoulders, your hands, as if they really had just let go of something heavy. Let them soften, in rhythm with your breath.
[pause 4s]
Now, one last step, a more delicate one. In some situations, we also carry part of the responsibility. A reaction that was too sharp, a silence, a boundary we didn't manage to set.
If that's the case for you, if part of this story belongs to you, look at it with the same gentleness.
You did what you could, with what you knew, with what you were feeling at the time. You can tell yourself: I forgive myself for my part, too. I'm learning.
And if no part of it is yours, which happens too, you can simply thank yourself for taking the time to look at all this.
If strong emotions come up, tears, sharp anger, let them pass through like a wave. That's normal. Breathe, come back to your feet, open your eyes if you need to.
[pause 3s]
Now stay for a few moments without doing anything. Notice your body. Your jaw, your chest, your belly. Is there a little more space than at the beginning? Or nothing different?
If there's a little space, breathe into it. A breath in that goes a little further. A breath out that sets down a little more.

And if nothing has changed, that's normal too. Letting go of a grudge is a process, not a switch. It happens in layers, like peeling an onion. You may need to come back to it several times. Each time, the weight gets a little lighter.
The anger may come back tomorrow. That isn't going backwards. It's just another layer showing itself.
On that day, you can simply come back to your feet, to your breath, and repeat the phrase that spoke to you today. No need to start from scratch.
Gently bring your attention back to the room. The sounds, the temperature of the air, the feel of your clothes against your skin.
Move your fingers and feet a little. Roll your shoulders, once or twice.
And when the moment is right for you, open your eyes.
If this story comes back to visit you today, remember the image of the bag set down on the ground. You don't have to carry it all the time. You have the right to feel freer.
And tonight, before you fall asleep, you can take one single breath and think: I'm putting it down, a little.

sessions.title: Loving-kindness
script: This practice is very old. It's called metta, or loving-kindness. It means offering wishes of well-being, first to yourself, then to wider and wider circles of people.
It isn't a way of forcing a feeling. You can't produce love on demand. You're simply watering a seed, and letting it grow at its own pace.
Research suggests that practicing this regularly may help people feel more connected to others, and a little gentler with themselves. Two precious things when stress pulls us into isolation.
Settle in comfortably. Your back upright but not rigid, as if a thread were gently drawing the top of your head toward the ceiling. Shoulders relaxed, hands resting.
Let your face soften. Your forehead, the space between your eyebrows, your cheeks. You can even let a faint smile appear at the corners of your mouth, if it comes naturally.
Breathe in through your nose.
[pause 3s]
And breathe out, a little longer.
Let that out-breath carry away a little of the day.
Once more. Breathe in… and breathe out, letting your body settle a little more.
Now bring your attention to the area of your heart, in the center of your chest. You can rest a hand there, if it helps you feel it.
Breathe as if the air were flowing in and out through that spot. You don't need to feel anything in particular. Just spend a little time there, with curiosity.
Throughout the practice, if your mind wanders, to your shopping list or tomorrow's meeting, that's normal. Simply come back to the phrases, without judging yourself.
And if a phrase passes by without you feeling it, that's fine. The next one arrives, like another wave.
[pause 3s]
We'll begin with you. It's often the hardest part, and that's exactly why we start there.
Picture yourself as you are right now, here, with your worries, your tiredness, your hopes. You can also picture the child you once were, if it's easier to feel tenderness toward them.
Choose whichever image brings the most softness. There's no right one.
Or think of the person who got through this week, with everything it asked of you. That person deserves kindness too.
And silently offer yourself these phrases, slowly, letting each one resonate.
May I be safe.
May I be peaceful.
May I be healthy.
May I live with ease.
You can imagine these words as a hand resting on your shoulder. Or as the voice of someone who loves you, saying them to you.
[pause 3s]
If the phrases feel mechanical, or a bit strange, that's very common. You can adapt them. May I be protected. May I find some calm. May I take care of my body. May my life feel a little lighter.
What matters isn't the exact wording, but the intention. The intention of wishing someone well. And that someone, for now, is you.
Once more, at your own pace. May I be safe. May I be peaceful. May I be healthy. May I live with ease.
Notice what happens inside. A little warmth, perhaps. Or resistance, a voice saying: I don't deserve this. If so, welcome that too. That voice needs kindness as well.
[pause 3s]

Now bring to mind someone you love easily. Someone whose name alone makes you smile. A loyal friend, a sister, a grandfather, a child. It can even be an animal, like the dog who greets you at the door every evening.
See them in front of you. Their face, their familiar expression, the way they move. Feel the tenderness that rises naturally when you think of them.
If memories come, a shared laugh, a hug on a station platform, let them feed the warmth.
Notice where you feel that tenderness in your body. In your chest, your hands, around your eyes. Let it spread a little.
And offer them these wishes, as if you were whispering them.
May you be safe.
May you be peaceful.
May you be healthy.
May you live with ease.
[pause 3s]
Imagine these wishes really reaching them. See them a little more relaxed, a little lighter. Maybe they smile, without knowing why.
Notice how easy it is with this person. How the warmth flows without effort. It's this same warmth that you can learn, little by little, to turn toward yourself and toward others.
Stay with that warmth for a breath or two before moving on.
Once more, for them. May you be safe. May you be peaceful. May you be healthy. May you live with ease.
[pause 3s]

Now think of a neutral person. Someone you see regularly but don't really know. The woman at the corner bakery. The morning bus driver. A neighbor you nod to on the stairs. A colleague from another floor.
If no one comes to mind, simply choose someone you passed today.
It doesn't matter if you can't picture them clearly. A rough outline is enough.

You know almost nothing about them. And yet, like you, this person has a whole life. People they love. Worries that wake them in the night. Small joys, disappointments. They too want to be happy. They too want to avoid suffering.
Think of everything you can't see. Maybe they slept badly. Maybe they're worried about a child, the rent, their health. Behind that ordinary face, there's a whole story.
Let yourself be curious about this person for a moment, the way you might wonder about a character in a book.
See their face, even if it's blurry. And offer them the same wishes.
May you be safe.
May you be peaceful.
May you be healthy.
May you live with ease.
[pause 3s]
You may feel less for this person. That's normal. You don't have to feel love. You're expressing an intention, and that intention counts.
Maybe the next time you see them, you'll look at them a little differently. With a little more curiosity, a little more warmth.
You can do this with anyone, really. It's a quiet practice you can take anywhere, in a queue or an open-plan office.
Now let your circle widen. Little by little.
You can imagine this warmth as a soft light that starts in your chest and spreads outward, circle after circle, like ripples on water when you drop in a pebble.
First, everyone in your building, or on your street. Those who are sleeping, those who are working, those who are cooking dinner.
Then your neighborhood, your city. People on the subway, in hospitals, in schools. Those who are happy right now, and those going through a hard time.
Including the people working through the night so others can sleep.
Then your country. Then every country. People getting up as you go to bed, people speaking languages you don't know.
Including people you'll never meet, whose lives are just as real as yours.
Let the light travel at its own speed. There's no need to picture everyone. The intention reaches further than your imagination.
And beyond humans, all living beings. Animals, birds, everything that breathes and, in one way or another, seeks to be well.
May all beings be safe.
May all beings be peaceful.
May all beings be healthy.
May all beings live with ease.
[pause 3s]
And don't forget that you're part of this great circle. These wishes come back to you too, like a wave returning to the shore.
If a strong emotion rises, sadness, joy, tears, that's normal. These practices sometimes touch tender places. You can pause, come back to your breathing, open your eyes.
Bring your hand back to your heart, if you like, and let a slightly longer out-breath help you settle.
Now let go of the phrases. Simply rest in whatever is here. Perhaps a warmth in your chest, a softness in your face, a sense of openness.
Or perhaps nothing special, and that's fine too. You've planted something. Seeds don't grow before our eyes.
Notice, too, that this kindness cost you nothing. You lost nothing by giving it. Often, the person offering it is the first to feel it.
Kindness isn't a limited supply. The more you practice it, the more easily it comes, for others and for yourself.
Let your breath come and go, like a calm wave. Enjoy this moment, without doing anything.
If you like, rest a hand on your heart again, and feel it beating beneath your palm. There's nothing to hold on to, and nothing to push away.
[pause 3s]
Take one more breath, just to savor this calm.
Gently, begin to come back. Take a slightly deeper breath.
Wiggle your fingers and toes. Stretch if you feel like it, slowly.
Listen to the sounds around you. Sense the room you're in.
And when the moment is right for you, open your eyes.
Today, if you pass someone in the street, at work, in a queue, you can silently send them one of these wishes. May you be peaceful. No one will know. And yet something will have shifted, in you.
And you can come back to this practice as often as you like, even for three minutes, on the bus or before you sleep.

sessions.title: A difficult person
script: There's probably someone in your life who tests you. A colleague who talks over you in meetings. A neighbor who makes noise at midnight. A brother-in-law with an opinion on everything. An ex you still have to coordinate with about the kids.
Just thinking about them, something may already be tightening. That's normal. These relationships cost us a lot of energy, often far beyond the time we actually spend with the person.
This practice won't change that person. Nor does it ask you to like them, or to accept everything. It offers something quieter: loosening, a little, the grip this relationship has on you.

To do that, we'll use loving-kindness, in several stages. First for yourself, then for someone you love. Only once you've built that solid base will we approach the difficult person. And always at your own pace.
Settle into a comfortable, stable position. Feet flat, back supported, hands resting on your thighs, palms up or down, whichever you prefer.
Close your eyes, or let your gaze rest on the floor, about a meter in front of you.
Take a full breath in through your nose.
[pause 3s]
And let it flow out through your mouth, slowly.
A second time. Breathe in… and breathe out, letting your shoulders move away from your ears.
One last time, at your own pace. Then let your breathing return to its natural rhythm.
Feel where your body is supported. Your feet, resting on the floor. Your thighs, on the seat. Your back, against the chair. Let your weight sink a little into whatever is holding you.
Then find your breath in one precise place. Maybe the cool air coming in through your nostrils. Maybe your belly rising and falling.
Keep this anchor in mind. If at any point the practice becomes too uncomfortable, you can always come back here: your feet on the floor, your breath coming and going.
Take a moment to really feel it. Maybe three breaths where you do nothing but notice the air coming in and going out. This is your home port.
[pause 3s]
We'll begin with you. Because you need to feel safe before venturing onto difficult ground. And because you, too, deserve kindness.
Place a hand on your heart, if that feels good. Feel its warmth.
And silently offer yourself these wishes, slowly.
May I find peace.
May I be free from fear.
May I take care of myself gently.
May I live with more lightness.
[pause 3s]
Let each phrase sink in, like a stone drifting slowly to the bottom of a lake. You don't need to feel anything strong. Just offer the intention.
Think of everything you're carrying right now. The responsibilities, the worries, the tiredness. And all the energy this difficult relationship takes from you, too.
Once more, for yourself. May I find peace. May I be free from fear. May I take care of myself gently. May I live with more lightness.
Notice whether these phrases warm anything, even slightly. And if it feels neutral, just keep the rhythm of the words, like a lullaby.
Imagine these wishes wrapping around you like a warm coat, one you'll keep on for the whole practice.
Now bring to mind someone you love easily. Someone with whom everything is simple. A friend, a child, a grandmother, a partner.
See their face. Their smile, their eyes. Imagine them sitting beside you, their presence warming you.
If it helps, remember one particular moment you shared. A laugh, a meal, a walk. Let that memory feed the warmth.
Notice the details: the light, the sounds, their laugh. The more concrete it is, the warmer it tends to feel.
Let the tenderness rise naturally. And offer them these wishes.
May you find peace.
May you be free from fear.
May you take care of yourself gently.
May you live with more lightness.
[pause 3s]
Notice how easily these words come for this person. Notice the warmth in your chest, maybe a smile. This warmth is your resource. You'll take it with you into the next stage.
Before going further, check in with how you feel. If you're already tired, or feeling raw, you can stay here, with this warmth. That's a complete practice in itself.

Now, if the moment feels right, we'll bring in the difficult person. One important note: choose someone moderately difficult. Not the person who has hurt you most in your life. Not someone who has put your safety at risk. Someone who irritates you, frustrates you, stresses you, but around whom you can stay safe.
If no one feels manageable enough today, you can stay with the person you love, or come back to yourself. That's completely valid.
Practicing with someone easier is still real practice. It builds the strength you'll need later.
If you've chosen someone, let their image appear. Not too close. You can imagine them on the far side of a room, or behind a pane of glass. You keep whatever distance suits you.
See their face. Their usual expression. Maybe a typical situation, a phrase they often say.
Remember, you can keep them at a distance. You're in charge of how close this gets.
[pause 3s]
Now notice what's happening in your body. Without changing anything.
Maybe your jaw clenches. Your stomach tightens. Your breathing gets shorter, or your chest closes. Maybe a flush of anger in your face, or an urge to get away.
Simply name what you observe. Irritation. Tension. Wariness. Weariness.
Naming it helps create a little room between you and the reaction.
Notice the thoughts that arrive, too. The reproaches, the things you wish you'd said, the scenes replaying in your head. You don't have to follow them. Recognize them, and come back to your body.
And offer yourself a little kindness, first. Your hand on your heart. A slow breath. You can tell yourself: this relationship is hard for me. My reaction makes sense.
If you like, breathe like this: breathing in, kindness for you. Breathing out, a little space around the tension.
[pause 3s]
Now, if you can, look at this person from a slightly different angle. Not to excuse their behavior. Just to see a little more widely.
This person, like you, has a body that gets tired. A heart that beats. Nights when they sleep badly.
Mornings when they wake up already worried.
They were a child once, too. A child who wanted to be loved, comforted, understood.
They may have worries you know nothing about. Fragile health, a relationship falling apart, enormous pressure at work, a difficult childhood.
Imagine them, for example, in the morning, in front of the mirror. Without their role, without their armor. Just someone starting their day, with their doubts.
Like you, they want to be happy. Like you, they want to avoid suffering. And often, their difficult behavior is a clumsy way of protecting themselves, or of coping with their own pain.
You don't have to find that fair. You can simply notice it: they're a human being too, with their wounds, just like me.
Take a breath with that idea. Notice whether anything shifts, even slightly, in your belly or your shoulders.
[pause 3s]
Now, if you feel able, try offering them some simple wishes. You can start with just one. And if it's too much, you can stop at any time.
May you find peace.
May you be free from what makes you suffer.
May you find a calmer way of being with others.
[pause 3s]
Take your time between each phrase. You can say them half-heartedly, without conviction. The intention matters more than the feeling.
Notice what that does. Maybe resistance, a voice saying: they don't deserve it. Maybe a small, unexpected loosening. Or both at once.
Keep one simple idea in mind. A person at peace generally does less harm to those around them. Wishing them peace is also, in a way, wishing yourself more peaceful relationships.
If the anger is too strong, you can go back to wishes for yourself: may I find peace around this person. May I be free from fear. That's a perfectly valid way to practice too.

And remember: wishing someone well doesn't stop you from setting clear boundaries. You can offer them these wishes and still say no, still protect yourself, still ask for respect. Kindness isn't the same as giving in.
If you can, offer these wishes once more, even half-heartedly. May you find peace. May you be free from what makes you suffer.
And if intense emotions come up, that's normal. These relationships often touch sensitive places. Come back to your feet, to your breath, open your eyes if you need to.
[pause 3s]
Now gently let the image of this person move away. They leave the room. You no longer need to hold them in mind.
Come back to yourself. Place both hands on your heart, or on your belly. Feel their warmth.
Let your hands tell your body: we're back with someone who's on our side.
Breathe slowly, and let your body know that this part is over. You're safe here.
You've just done something brave. You looked directly at a relationship that weighs on you, and brought a little openness to it, however small.
Offer yourself these wishes one last time. May I find peace. May I be free from fear. May I take care of myself gently. May I live with more lightness.
[pause 3s]
Stay in this space for a few moments, without doing anything. Notice your body now. Your jaw, your belly, your shoulders. Is there a difference from the moment that person first appeared?
Maybe a little more space. Maybe nothing in particular. That's okay. This kind of practice often works over time, in small touches.
Whatever you notice, you can meet it with the same kindness you offered yourself at the start.
Notice, too, what you've learned about yourself. Perhaps a need that isn't being respected in this relationship. Calm, recognition, space. That need deserves your attention.
The next time you see this person, you don't have to act any differently. But you may feel just a little more distance. Half a second more before you react. That can change everything.
Because in that half second, you get to choose your response, instead of simply reacting.
And if this relationship ever becomes truly too heavy, or causes you lasting pain, you also have the right to seek support, from someone close or from a professional.
[pause 3s]
Gently, bring your attention back to your breath. Then to the room. The sounds, the light behind your eyelids, the temperature of the air.
Wiggle your fingers and toes. Stretch, if you feel like it.
And when the moment is right for you, open your eyes.
Today, if this person puts you on edge again, try to remember, silently: they want to be happy too, just like me. And give yourself, first of all, one kind breath.
